answer:
Recommendation: migrate in a strangler pattern over the quarter, keeping the monolith's login as the source of truth until the final cutover, and use the identity provider's credential-migration hook (lazy, verify-on-login migration) so no password is ever reset. The monolith stays authoritative for sessions and credentials until a late, reversible flip; only the last step is hard to undo, and we defer it to the end of the quarter with a rehearsed rollback.

Phase 1 (weeks 1-2): Put a reverse proxy or auth shim in front of the login endpoint and session check, with a feature flag per user cohort. Nothing changes for users; the shim passes everything through to the monolith. Reversible by flipping the flag off. True afterwards: all logins still hit the monolith, instrumentation shows baseline traffic.

Phase 2 (weeks 3-4): Configure the hosted provider as an OIDC client of nothing yet: create the application, realms, and the migration hook endpoint, but route no users to it. Build the hook as a server-side endpoint in the monolith that accepts username and password, checks the bcrypt hash locally, and returns success or failure. Test with internal accounts only. True afterwards: provider is configured, hook works for staff, no customer impact.

Phase 3 (weeks 5-7): Pilot the OIDC login path for a 1% cohort of internal and then external users. On each successful login through the provider, the provider's migration hook calls the monolith to verify the bcrypt password; on success the provider stores its own hash (its native algorithm) and the user is marked migrated. The monolith still creates its own session as well, so either side can be rolled back. Ramp to 10%, 50%, 100% of new logins over the following weeks, watching error rates and lockouts. True afterwards: users who log in are migrated lazily, each one reversible by flag.

Users who do not log in during the quarter are not forced to reset. Their credentials stay in the monolith's bcrypt table and remain valid, because the hook verifies against that table on their first login whenever it happens, even months later. To avoid a long tail of unmigrated users blocking the final cutover, run a bulk migration job during quiet hours that, for each unmigrated user, uses the provider's bulk import API with the bcrypt hash (most providers accept bcrypt natively, which avoids needing the plaintext). Verify a sample of imports by checking that the provider accepts the password for a test account. Bulk import can be reversed per batch by deleting the imported records, which is safe because the monolith still holds the originals.

Sessions while both systems are live: the monolith keeps its server-side session store, and the shim issues a session cookie for each login regardless of which system authenticated the user. A user logged in through the provider receives an OIDC token and also a monolith session, linked by a session identifier in the token claims. Logout must clear both: the shim revokes the provider session and deletes the monolith session. Token lifetimes are kept short (for example fifteen minutes with refresh) so that a rollback does not leave long-lived tokens valid against a system that no longer trusts them. Session cookie domains and SameSite settings must be tested so that the shim and monolith agree on which session is current.

Point of no return: the step after which the monolith no longer issues sessions or accepts passwords for login, and the provider becomes the only authority. We reach it only after every active user has been migrated (verified by the bulk job and a count of users without a provider identity), after the monolith login path has run in shadow mode for at least two weeks with zero divergence, and after a full rollback has been rehearsed in staging within the one-hour budget. The cutover itself is a flag flip; the irreversible part is deleting the monolith's password column and session store, which we do only after a further two-week soak. Until that deletion, rollback remains a flag flip plus re-enabling the monolith login path.

Cleanup after the point of no return: once the soak period passes, remove the monolith's login and session code, drop or archive the bcrypt password column (encrypted backup retained per the retention policy), delete the migration hook and bulk-import tooling, remove the proxy shim, and revoke any stale monolith session tokens. Retain the bcrypt table in an archived, access-restricted form for a defined period in case of a support dispute.

Open questions and caveats to resolve in week one: whether the provider accepts bcrypt hashes natively or requires a custom hash scheme; the provider's rate limits and whether bulk import can run at 40,000 records within an acceptable window; how account recovery (email reset) is handled during coexistence; whether any service-to-service callers use the monolith session directly and would break at cutover; and the staffing reality of three part-time engineers, which argues for cutting scope (for example, deferring social login) rather than the reversibility and soak periods, which should not be shortened.
